GraceChangeDesignContext.Rationale:
Search is intentionally modeled as a provider capability rather than as a property of the omnibox or browser engine. The future shell decides whether text is a URL, command or search query. A selected search provider receives only the already-classified query and returns a navigation target. A separate browser.navigate call performs the mutation.
This preserves two important Worldline boundaries. First, CEF does not own product policy such as which search engine is preferred. Second, a plugin allowed to see search text does not automatically receive authority to mutate a page. Search resolution and browser navigation therefore remain separate admissions with separate outcomes.
The first provider implementation should be deliberately boring: a structured fixed web origin/path plus one query parameter and bounded static parameters. That covers the common browser-search case while avoiding arbitrary URL templating and string concatenation. Multiple installations of the same plugin definition can represent different search engines, which directly exercises the runtime's existing multiple-installation and provider-selection model.
GraceChangeDesignContext.ArchitectureSketch:
shell / command surface / agent | | browser.search/resolve v generic capability broker + provider selection | v selected worldline-browser-search installation | | returns SearchNavigationTarget v caller chooses whether to invoke browser.navigate | v BrowserEngineProvider / CEF
Important: the search provider never receives implicit NavigatePage authority and never calls CEF directly.

KeyDesignDecisions.Decision: `browser.search/0.1` is a target-resolution capability, not a navigation capability and not a structured SERP/search-results API.
Address-versus-search classification belongs to the later shell/command layer. The provider must not guess whether `localhost:3000`, `rust book` or `2+2` is an address, command or search.

Provider selection should reuse generic capability provider discovery and selection. Search does not justify a browser-specific registry in the kernel. If durable explicit user selection cannot be expressed by the current generic mechanism, that is a platform design question to surface during planning rather than something to hide in CEF or UI code.

The first provider is installation-configurable. Multiple installations of one definition are preferable to duplicating nearly identical binaries for every conventional URL-based search engine. Provider branding/catalog metadata can remain installation/plugin metadata and does not need to enter the engine-neutral search DTO.

The first URL builder is structural rather than template-string based. A provider owns a fixed parsed origin/path, one explicit query parameter name and bounded static query parameters. User search text is inserted only as the value of that query parameter through a URL library.
Production providers use HTTPS. Loopback HTTP exists solely to make deterministic and real-CEF acceptance tests independent of the public Internet.
Search query text is treated as sensitive payload. Generic Worldline audit may record provider identity, operation name, timing and outcome, but not the query body by default.

Alternatives.Alternative: Hard-code the selected search URL in the omnibox. Rejected because it makes shell code depend on a vendor, prevents ordinary provider replacement and mixes future UI parsing with search-provider policy.
Add search to CEF or BrowserEngineProvider. Rejected because CEF already provides navigation primitives; choosing a search engine is product policy, not an engine primitive.

Let a search provider navigate directly. Rejected because query disclosure and page mutation have different authority and failure semantics. Returning a target also keeps the provider useful to non-browser consumers and tests.

Make v0.1 a remote JSON search API returning titles, snippets and ranked results. Rejected for the first slice because that introduces network credentials, provider-specific schemas, ranking semantics, pagination, result provenance, privacy and rate-limit policy that are unnecessary for the basic browser-search journey.

Use arbitrary `{searchTerms}` URL templates. Not selected initially because raw templating creates more parser/injection surface than the common case requires. A later additive provider implementation can support path or richer templates if actual provider needs justify it.

Store a browser-specific default provider table in the kernel. Rejected because provider identity/selection is already a generic plugin-runtime concern and because the kernel must remain browser-agnostic.

SecurityAndPrivacy.Point: The caller needs explicit search-resolution authority because invocation discloses user-entered text to the selected provider installation.
The search provider does not need NavigatePage, ActOnPage, cookies, storage, download, request-policy or DevTools authority for the v0.1 operation.
The provider response is data, not authority. Possessing a URL does not bypass normal navigation admission.
Query-derived bytes cannot influence target scheme, credentials, hostname or path in the first implementation. Only the query-parameter value varies.
Oversized input/config/result values fail before navigation and before unbounded allocation or logging.
Provider crash or quarantine must not degrade direct URL navigation. Search is optional composition, not browser availability infrastructure.

GraceChangeDesignContext.ProviderSelectionModel:
The preferred proving topology is two installations of `worldline-browser-search` with the same capability contract and different installation-owned configuration. The generic broker/provider-selection layer selects installation A or B. The caller contains no `if google`, `if yandex` or equivalent provider-name branching.
Provider provenance should come from the invocation/provider-selection metadata that Worldline already owns rather than from a self-asserted provider name embedded in the result DTO. This keeps audit identity authoritative and prevents response data from impersonating another provider.
GraceChangeDesignContext.TestingModel:
S3E should use two deterministic loopback provider configurations. Resolving a query must cause zero origin requests. The test then separately invokes normal browser navigation with the returned target and verifies exactly one expected request with the decoded query value.
The real Windows variant should stage the pinned CEF runtime, use the native provider process, reject ReferenceBrowserBackend substitution and prove that the same engine-neutral search result feeds the ordinary navigation path. No public search service is contacted by acceptance tests.

DeferredDecisions.Decision: The exact persistent mechanism for a user-selected preferred provider is deferred to the plan after inspecting current generic provider-selection state. If the generic mechanism is sufficient, search adds no selector store. If it is insufficient, the plan must stop/replan rather than silently introduce browser-specific selection into the kernel or CEF.
A seed catalog of conventional providers may be shipped after the neutral capability is proven. The exact provider list and default are product policy, not normative architecture in this change.
Remote suggestions/autocomplete may later become a separate capability with its own privacy, cancellation, debounce and network policy.
Structured web-search result APIs may later use a separate `search.results` family rather than overloading `browser.search/resolve`.

Workspace/history/semantic retrieval remains separate. A future unified command surface may aggregate many providers, but aggregation is a shell or higher-level search-composition concern, not a reason to merge their source of truth or authority.

The current branch still exposes a stale active request-policy correction bundle while later state treats that slice as completed. That lifecycle inconsistency is an explicit prerequisite for plan approval/execution and is not silently repaired by this design context.

Scenarios.Scenario: A caller with search-resolution authority asks provider A to resolve `rust async book`. The provider returns an HTTPS navigation target but no page changes until the caller separately receives navigation authority and invokes browser.navigate.
The user switches from provider A to provider B. The same consumer invokes the same `browser.search/0.1` operation and receives B's target without code changes or a new browser-engine path.

A malicious query containing percent signs, ampersands, fragments, Unicode and text resembling a new scheme remains data inside the configured query parameter and cannot replace the fixed scheme/host/path.
The selected provider crashes. Search becomes unavailable or is reselected by generic provider policy, while direct navigation and unrelated browser services continue working.

A deterministic real-CEF S3E run resolves a loopback target, records zero requests before navigation, performs a separate authorized navigation and records exactly the expected origin request afterward.
